newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Wet Argentine December good for soy, slows wheat.
newsitem.headline: Wet Argentine December good for soy, slows wheat.

text.p: Heavy rains in Argentina's grain belt have slowed the wheat harvest and raised concerns over possible crop damage but have raised soil moisture to perfect levels for other crops, traders said Wednesday.

"In some places in the south of Buenos Aires it has rained 500 millimeters in five days," said one trader, who had just returned from a tour of the grain belt. He said most of the wheat was in very good shape but there was a danger plants could be washed out and suffer loss of protein if it rained much more.

He was forecasting 15.5 million tonnes of wheat. But another trader told Reuters he was forecasting more than 16 million tonnes, and added "there are those in the market who are not ruling out 17 million tonnes."

He said that he did not think there had been damage to the wheat crop so far and that, while harvesting has been slowed, the ports have enough grain stockpiled and waiting in trucks to keep working briskly for a while.
Good weather has led market players to steadily raise their forecasts for wheat output, which will be up from about 9.2 million tonnes in drought-blighted 1995/96.
The government expects exports to more than double to around 10 million tonnes and said Monday that commitments to foreign buyers had already reached 5.7 million tonnes.

The biggest taker was traditional customer Brazil, with 1.0 million tonnes, but buyers included destinations unusually far afield for Argentine wheat such as Bulgaria, which has signed up for 420,000 tonnes.
The first trader enthused about conditions for oilseed.
"The bottom line is that now soil moisture is excellent more or less everywhere. We only need it to stop raining for sowing to continue," he said.
"All we need is a few dry days to sow the beans. You cannot sow them when it's muddy."

He thought four-fifths of the single crop soybeans were already in the ground, but the sowing of the second crop, which is planted after wheat is harvested in the same ground, was awaiting the end of the rain. He said that about half the soybeans would be second crop this year.

Using an estimate for soybean area of about 6.1-6.2 million hectares, he said eventual output could be close to 13 million tonnes. The government, estimating planted area at 6.3 million hectares, says it expects 13.4 million tonnes.
He said the sunflower crop was in very good shape and that output should be around 5.2 million tonnes. The government estimates 5.3 million tonnes.
The second trader said he thought there would be 13-14 million tonnes of soybeans.

The lastest figures from the government's Agricultural Secretariat put wheat harvesting 22.8 percent complete by November 29. Soybean sowing was 32.5 percent complete, sunflower sowing 87.2 percent complete and maize sowing 78.5 percent over.
